## Project scope

`taxodist` is an open-source project for retrieving ordered taxonomic lineages and measuring separation between nodes in a classification hierarchy. It is available as coordinated R, Python, and Julia packages and through an interactive web application.

The project addresses a practical need: a reproducible way to resolve taxon names, inspect their lineages, identify their most recent common ancestor, and construct labeled distance objects for downstream analysis.

By default, lineages come from [The Taxonomicon](http://taxonomicon.taxonomy.nl), based on *Systema Naturae 2000*. Since version 1.1.0, they can also be retrieved from the [Open Tree of Life reference taxonomy](https://tree.opentreeoflife.org/about/taxonomy-version) and the [NCBI Taxonomy](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/taxonomy) (see [Taxonomic sources](sources.qmd)). The external sources remain responsible for the underlying classifications; `taxodist` retrieves, cleans, organizes, and compares those records.

## Methodological position

By default, the distance between distinct hierarchy nodes is the reciprocal of MRCA depth. Identical complete lineages receive distance zero. Within a connected hierarchy, this produces an ultrametric. Path-length, Wu–Palmer, and rank-based distances are available as explicit alternatives.

These values measure classification depth. They do not estimate evolutionary time, genetic or morphological divergence, phylogenetic branch length, or statistical support for ancestry. The interpretation of every analysis is conditional on the source classification and the intermediate nodes it records.

Version 0.6.0 formalized this distinction across the R package, Python package, application, reference data, and documentation. Version 0.7.0 optimized cached matrix construction. Version 0.8.0 added auditable resolution records, offline user-supplied classifications, and portable analysis bundles shared by all three implementations. Version 0.9.0 corrected retrieval and caching errors and added classification trees, distances between two sets of taxa, and the comparison of repeated analyses. Version 1.0.0, the first stable release, replaced the text-based lineage parser with one that reads the structure of each Taxonomicon page, retained the rank of every node, added alternative distance metrics and the taxonomic distinctness indices of Clarke and Warwick, and froze the metric definitions and the bundle format for the 1.x series. Version 1.1.0 added the Open Tree and NCBI taxonomies as alternative lineage sources, the comparison of analyses across sources, and community analyses: the taxonomic dissimilarities of Clarke, Somerfield and Chapman between samples and the NRI and NTI effect sizes of Webb et al.

## Project history

The project began with a general question: how can the shared hierarchical position of any two named organisms be retrieved and compared programmatically?

Early development focused on resolving names and parsing the deeply nested classification exposed by The Taxonomicon. Subsequent releases added matrix operations, lineage comparison, cache persistence, visualization, multivariate helpers, offline reference data, Python and Julia implementations with matching distance semantics, and diversity indices.

The project remains deliberately focused on classification-based analysis. It does not attempt to replace curated phylogenies, sequence-based inference, divergence-time estimation, or specialized taxonomic name services.

## Reproducibility and transparency

Live taxonomic databases change. Analyses using retrieved lineages should therefore record:

- the `taxodist` version and implementation;
- the retrieval date;
- the lineage source (and, for the Open Tree Taxonomy, its version, which resolutions and bundles record);
- the selected identifiers (numeric Taxonomicon IDs or prefixed Open Tree and NCBI IDs), particularly for homonyms;
- unresolved or excluded taxa;
- whether live data or the packaged `taxobase` reference object was used;
- the distance metric and downstream analysis settings.

The fixed `taxobase` object is distributed for examples, tests, and comparisons that must not depend on current server availability. It should not be assumed to represent the latest live classification.

## Citation

The R, Python, and Julia implementations are parts of the same software project and may be cited with a common project-level reference:

> Villa, R. F. (2026). *taxodist: Taxonomic Hierarchy Distances and Lineage Analysis* (version {{< var version >}}). Open-source software. <https://taxodist.github.io/>.

In the methods section, identify the implementation used:

- R package: <https://cran.r-project.org/package=taxodist>
- Python package: <https://pypi.org/project/taxodist/>
- Julia package: <https://platform.juliahub.com/ui/Packages/General/Taxodist/>

The R command below returns the citation metadata distributed with the package:

```r
citation("taxodist")
```

### BibTeX

The entries below are those returned by `toBibtex(citation("taxodist"))` for version 1.1.0, with citation keys added. Cite the first entry together with the source of your lineages: The Taxonomicon by default, the Open Tree Taxonomy or the NCBI Taxonomy when `source = "ott"` or `"ncbi"`. Use the copy button to paste them into a `.bib` file.

```bibtex
@Manual{taxodist,
  title = {taxodist: Taxonomic Hierarchy Distances and Lineage Analysis},
  author = {Rodrigo Fonseca Villa},
  year = {2026},
  note = {R package version 1.1.0},
  url = {https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=taxodist},
}

@Misc{taxonomicon,
  title = {The Taxonomicon: Systema Naturae 2000},
  author = {Sheila J. Brands},
  year = {1989},
  note = {Continuously updated taxonomic database},
  url = {http://taxonomicon.taxonomy.nl},
}

@Article{rees2017,
  title = {Automated assembly of a reference taxonomy for phylogenetic data synthesis},
  author = {Jonathan A. Rees and Karen Cranston},
  journal = {Biodiversity Data Journal},
  year = {2017},
  volume = {5},
  pages = {e12581},
  doi = {10.3897/BDJ.5.e12581},
}

@Article{schoch2020,
  title = {NCBI Taxonomy: a comprehensive update on curation, resources and tools},
  author = {Conrad L. Schoch and others},
  journal = {Database},
  year = {2020},
  volume = {2020},
  pages = {baaa062},
  doi = {10.1093/database/baaa062},
}
```

The source repositories also provide language-specific citation and release metadata.

### Classification sources

Published analyses should also cite the classification their lineages come from (`taxo_sources()` lists the citations, and every resolution and bundle records its source).

The Taxonomicon (`source = "taxonomicon"`, the default; also the source of the packaged `taxobase` lineages):

> Brands, S.J. (1989 onwards). *Systema Naturae 2000*. Amsterdam, The Netherlands. Retrieved from The Taxonomicon, <http://taxonomicon.taxonomy.nl>.

The Open Tree Taxonomy (`source = "ott"`); also report the taxonomy version recorded in the resolution or bundle:

> Rees, J.A. & Cranston, K. (2017). Automated assembly of a reference taxonomy for phylogenetic data synthesis. *Biodiversity Data Journal* 5, e12581. <https://doi.org/10.3897/BDJ.5.e12581>

The NCBI Taxonomy (`source = "ncbi"`):

> Schoch, C.L. et al. (2020). NCBI Taxonomy: a comprehensive update on curation, resources and tools. *Database* 2020, baaa062. <https://doi.org/10.1093/database/baaa062>

The software citation acknowledges the implementation; the source citation acknowledges the classification data. Neither should replace the other.
